blocks.text: Over the last quarter, the global macroeconomic and aviation landscape continued to be shaped by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East that began in late February 2026. Below we have summarized where we believe the aviation industry stands as of Q2 2026.

items: Middle East Conflict & Fuel Prices: Jet fuel prices have remained elevated through the quarter, with IATA now expecting jet fuel to average $152 per barrel for the full year 2026, a nearly 70% increase over the $90 per barrel average recorded in 2025.¹ Unlike COVID-19, this remains a cost and network shock rather than a demand collapse, and passenger appetite has continued to prove resilient. The ceasefire announced in late April remained in place as of the end of Q2, although it has since expired. Though disruption to Middle East carriers persists, we continue to monitor developments and believe that the Fund's asset-backed, long-term lease structure may provide meaningful insulation from near-term fuel price volatility.

Airline Profitability: Airline profitability has come under material pressure, with IATA revising its full-year 2026 net profit forecast down to $23Bn at a 2.0% net margin, roughly half its pre- conflict projection of $41Bn and 3.9%.¹ Demand fundamentals, however, remain robust: IATA still expects a record 84% load factor for the year, up from 83.5% in 2025.¹ We believe this divergence between record demand and compressed margins reflects a cost crisis for airline owners rather than a demand crisis for aircraft – a dynamic that favors well-positioned lessors, whose lease income remains contractually insulated from airline-level margin pressure.2

Supply / Demand: The global order backlog remains near record levels, with IATA reporting more than 18,000 aircraft on order as of May 2026, representing over half of the active global fleet.¹ The conflict has only deepened this imbalance; supply chain disruptions continue to delay fleet renewal, airlines are extending the lives of existing aircraft and increasing utilization in response, and the window during which carriers must rely on leased in-service aircraft continues to extend – dynamics we believe are generally supportive of our strategy.

blocks.text: Aircraft Fund & Business Update

items: Since the Fund's initial closing in April 2025, we have secured over $350M of capital commitments. We are actively advancing discussions with a number of prospective investors and anticipate a meaningfully-sized final close in October.

Q2 2026 activity centered on opportunistically monetizing existing assets while we believe the portfolio continued to perform strongly. We remain proactive in identifying monetization opportunities where pricing is attractive and accretive for investors. As of Q2 2026, the Fund has closed one aircraft monetization and has five additional assets in the process of being monetized, all of which we estimate will generate attractive gains upon closing in Q3 and Q4 of this year.3

This activity builds on a portfolio of aircraft acquired in Q1 2026, funded at Q2 quarter end. These aircraft were subsequently included in the platform's second Master Trust ABS issuance, completed in June for $568M.

Through Q2 2026, the Fund is tracking above our high-single-digit distributable cash yield target. Capital called to date represents 36% of equity commitments, reflecting the Q1 2026 aircraft portfolio acquisition described above. We are actively evaluating several new investments for the Fund and remain committed to growing the portfolio with discipline.

blocks.html: PERFORMANCE CALCULATIONS METHODOLOGIES 1. Multiple of Money (MoM) is equal to the total value for each investment divided by the investment amount for such investment. The net multiples of money with respect to each Bain Capital fund presented are calculated as the sum of the distributions made to non-affiliated institutional investors of such Bain Capital fund and the remaining capital balances of such institutional investors, divided by the contributions of such institutional investors. Net multiple of money reflects management fees, fund expenses, carried interest allocations and priority profits, where applicable, while gross multiple of money does not. 2. Gross multiple of money returns for individual investments and funds shown do not reflect fund level expenses and fees borne by investors, which will have the effect of reducing returns and in the aggregate, are expected to be substantial. 3. Gross Multiple of Money returns for individual investments shown do not reflect origination fees, advisory fees, performance allocations, taxes, transaction costs incurred in connection with the disposition of investments and other expenses to be borne by investors, which will have the effect of reducing returns and in the aggregate and may be substantial. In addition, since fund-level Gross MoM returns are calculated based on individual investment cash flows and Net MoM returns are calculated based on the methodology described in Note 1 above, the calculations and resulting returns could differ, particularly with respect to the use and existence of a fund subscription line at the end of a reporting period. While it is expected that the Gross MoM and Net MoM methodologies, aside from the impact of fees, expenses and carried interest allocations with respect to Net MoM, will converge over time with the paydown of any applicable fund subscription line, differences in return methodologies will exist at any given reporting period during the life of the fund. To the extent that amounts are outstanding on a fund subscription line at a given time, this could result in Net MoM returns being higher than would have been the case in the absence of such borrowing.

Specifically, IRR is the discount rate at which the net present value of all cash flows and any remaining investment value is equal to zero. In other words, IRR is the discount rate at which the (i) present value of all capital invested in an investment (including expenses specifically allocable to the investment) is equal to (ii) the present value of all returns from the investment (whether or not realized). 5. In certain vehicles Bain Capital Special Situations has deferred portions of carried interest accrual to the General Partner as contemplated within the applicable vehicle’s legal documents. IRRs shown include all returns generated by reinvested capital and profit. 8. Annualized returns are computed based on the change in value during the period of a theoretical investment made at the beginning of the period. The change in value of a theoretical investment is measured by comparing the aggregate ending value of Limited Partners with the aggregate beginning value adjusted for cash flows related to capital contributions or withdrawals during the period. Returns are geometrically linked on a monthly basis. 9. Fund-level gross and net IRRs are calculated based on the timing and values of cash flows from limited partners. The methodology used for calculating the fund-level gross and net IRR is consistent. 10. Differences in IRRs will depend on a number of factors including the amount borrowed by the Partnership, the timing of repayments of the credit facilities, as well as the applicable interest amounts under the credit facilities.

blocks.html: The Vintage 1 and Vintage 2 Portfolios are distinct groups of aircrafts owned by the Bain Capital and Griffin Global Asset Management platform. Vintage 1 and Vintage 2 are owned by different Bain Capital Special Situations’ Funds though all aircraft across Vintages are held within a corporate entity where any related financing is comingled, i.e. the Bain Capital / Griffin Platform. Further details on the portfolio are noted below. 1. Vintage 1: The portfolio’s first aircraft was acquired on January 7, 2021 and is owned primarily by the Global Special Situations I and Special Situations Asia I. 2. Vintage 2: The portfolio’s first aircraft was acquired on September 23, 2022 and is owned primarily by the Global Special Situations II and Special Situations Asia II. 3. Combined returns for Vintage 1 and Vintage 2 are extracted performance across multiple funds and may be deemed to be “hypothetical” performance. Hypothetical performance is subject to inherent limitations, as the performance may have been different had the investments been selected to occur in one fund. 4. Net returns were calculated using the following assumptions and in line with the undiscounted Aircraft Fund fees and expenses reflected in the offering documents: a) Management fees are based on the weighted average life of the investments multiplied by the total invested capital multiplied by 1.50%. b) Carried interest percentage is 20% c) Operating expenses are based on the weighted average life of the investments multiplied by the total invested capital multiplied by 0.25%
